parts.title: Meeting an astronaut
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month, our school had an unusual visitor: a real astronaut. Her name was Commander Joanna Reid, and she had spent five months on the International Space Station. Everyone in the school hall was silent when she walked on stage.

She began by showing us a short film of life in space. We saw her floating in the air and drinking water from a bubble. When she turned upside down, the whole hall laughed. Then she explained that the hardest thing was not the danger but the loneliness. 'I missed my family,' she told us, 'and I missed the smell of rain.'

After the talk, we were allowed to ask questions. A little boy in the front asked what astronauts eat for breakfast, and she answered that she had often eaten porridge from a bag. My friend Anil asked whether she was ever afraid, and she said that she was most afraid before the launch, not during it.

At the end, she told us that anyone could work for a space agency, not only brilliant scientists. 'You need patience and teamwork,' she said. I went home thinking about it all evening, and I have already decided to study physics.

questions.explanation: It showed her floating and drinking water from a bubble in space.

questions.explanation: She said the hardest thing was the loneliness.

options: She was never afraid at all
She was most afraid before the launch

questions.explanation: She was most afraid before the launch, not during it.

options: Patient people who work in teams
questions.explanation: She says you need patience and teamwork.

questions.explanation: He has already decided to study physics.

parts.title: A short history of space travel
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
People have always looked up at the sky and wondered what was out there. [1] The first rocket to leave the Earth's atmosphere was launched in 1944, but nobody travelled in it.

The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin, a Russian pilot, who orbited the Earth in 1961. [2] The whole journey lasted only one hour and forty-eight minutes, but it changed history.

Eight years later, in July 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. [3] About six hundred million people watched on television as he stepped onto the grey dust.

Since then, scientists have sent machines to Mars, Jupiter and even beyond the solar system. [4] Today, astronauts live on a space station for months at a time, and companies are planning holidays in space. [5] Some people believe that one day humans will live on other planets.
sentences: Armstrong later became a university professor.
Many dreamed of travelling there, but it took until the twentieth century to do it.
Some of these machines are still sending pictures today.
He was only twenty-seven years old.
Ideas like these once seemed like science fiction.
His landing was shown live all over the world.

gaps.explanation: "Travelling there" and "the twentieth century" lead to the first rocket in 1944.
His age is extra information about Gagarin before the length of the journey.
"Shown live" explains why millions of people watched on television.
"These machines" refers to the machines sent to other planets.
"Ideas like these" refers to space holidays, which once seemed like science fiction.

My sister, who is [3] interested in stars than I am, wanted to look at Jupiter. We [4] the sky for about ten minutes, but there were too many clouds. I am going to try again [5] the sky is clear. I will [6] you a photograph by email when I get a good one.

parts.title: A night at the observatory
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: hadrian
turns.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome to Hilltop Observatory. Tonight, we are open from eight until eleven o'clock. Please speak quietly, and switch off your phones, because the light from the screens makes it hard for your eyes to see in the dark. First, we will look at the Moon, which is almost full this evening. Then we will point the telescope at Saturn. Our telescope is one hundred years old, and its mirror is thirty centimetres wide. Each person can look for two minutes, so please be patient. Afterwards, there is hot chocolate in the café for one pound fifty. If you would like to come again, our next open night is on the fourth of March.

gaps.explanation: The observatory is open until eleven o'clock.
He asks visitors to switch off their phones.

gaps.prompt: The first thing to look at is the ___
gaps.explanation: First, they will look at the Moon.
The mirror is thirty centimetres wide.

gaps.prompt: Each person can look for ___ minutes
gaps.explanation: Each person can look for two minutes.
Hot chocolate is one pound fifty.

parts.title: A young astronomer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: Today I'm speaking to Dr Kavya Menon, a young astronomer. Kavya, how did you become interested in space?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: When I was nine, my uncle gave me a small telescope for my birthday. The first time I saw the rings of Saturn, I could not believe that they were real.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What is the hardest part of your work?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Working through the night. Telescopes work best in the dark, so I often sleep in the daytime. My friends say I live like a vampire.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What do you do on a normal day?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Mostly, I sit at a computer and study pictures sent by telescopes. I look for tiny changes that show something is moving or exploding.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: Which object in the sky do you like best?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Still Saturn. I have seen thousands of beautiful pictures, but nothing has ever made me feel the way that first look did.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What advice do you have for beginners?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Look at the sky every night, and learn the names of a few stars. You do not need an expensive telescope to begin.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: And what do you hope to do in the future?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: I want to be part of a team that finds planets around other stars, planets where life might be possible.
